transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Michael Torres (AcornBank Head of Platform), Linda Park (AcornBank CISO), Derek Huang (AcornBank ML Engineer), Sonia Rivera (AcornBank Procurement)

Auto-generated summary (may be rough): Discussed dedicated reserved capacity for inference, isolation needs, burst/bursting to hosted, security & KMS, next steps to run benchmarks.

00:00 Alex Chen (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on this account. Samira and Jordan from our SE team are with me. How's everyone doing?
00:08 Michael Torres (AcornBank): Good, thanks Alex. We're excited to dig into the dedicated option, we've, um, been running some pilots on the hosted API but traffic's ramping and we need isolation.
00:18 Linda Park (CISO): Hi all. I'll be listening for the security bits, especially around key management and audit logs.
00:24 Alex: Great, quick agenda: we want to understand your workload patterns, isolation requirements (VPC/private), burst strategy, scaling expectations, and then sync on next steps for pricing and benchmarks. Sound good?
00:34 Derek Huang (ML Eng): Yep, sounds good. I'll try to hold questions until the end but might chime in.
00:40 Jordan (Redwood SE): We'll also talk about common trade-offs — latency vs cost, persistent KV caching, quantization options, and autoscale.

02:05 Michael: Quick context — AcornBank is moving from proof-of-concept to production in two apps: a customer support summarization flow and a real-time fraud cueing assistant. Summaries are batch (higher latency OK), fraud assistant is low-latency, p95 target ~150ms for inference. Today we hit ~150 reqs/s baseline, peaks to 700 reqs/s around end-of-day processing and specific campaigns.
02:30 Alex: Helpful. When you say 700 at peak, is that sustained or short bursts?
02:35 Michael: Mostly short bursts, 5-20 minutes, but occasionally several hours during campaign spikes.
02:40 Samira: That's helpful — we typically recommend a dedicated pool sized for consistent baseline with burst capacity to hosted or reserved burst nodes. For low-latency flows we can pre-warm and use continuous batching but keep per-request latency tight.

05:00 Linda: From security side we need VPC isolation, customer-managed KMS (or HSM), audit logs for every inference request and model version pinning. Data residency must stay in our AWS region, and we need SOC 2 Type II evidence.
05:20 Alex: Totally reasonable. Our Private and Dedicated offerings support VPC peering, bring-your-own-KMS (YMMV with on-prem HSM but we have integrations), and we provide audit logs; we'll include SOC2 docs.
05:30 Linda: Also interested in RBAC for model access, and can we restrict which models are allowed in the tenant?
05:36 Samira: Yes, model allowlists and version pinning are supported. RBAC is configurable — we can walk through roles.

07:10 Derek: On the ML side, two quick details: models are a 7B LLM for summaries and a 13B distilled model for fraud assistant. We run quantized weights for cost reasons; how does Redwood handle quantized models and KV cache across shards?
07:28 Jordan: We support a variety of quantization profiles; runtime selects kernels and execution paths optimized for quantized weights. KV cache is managed per-session and can be persisted across requests to avoid repeated prefix computation — there are trade-offs around memory. The SE team will map your sequence length distribution to expected memory and throughput.

10:00 Michael: For sizing, what's the usual unit? GPUs, or vCPU equivalents? We need firm guidance to budget for reserved capacity.
10:10 Samira: We size by equivalent GPU capacity and throughput targets. For example, a p95 150ms on your 13B model at X concurrency might need Y A100-equivalent GPUs. We'll provide a sizing worksheet where you input batch sizes, concurrency, and p95 targets and we output recommended reserved GPUs and expected qps.

12:45 Linda: On compliance, does Redwood offer contract language around data handling? We also prefer no long-term retention of request payloads.
12:55 Alex: Yes — retention policy configurable, and we can include contractual clauses about data handling. We'll surface the legal/contract playbook and standard DPA language.

15:20 Michael: A big concern is burst strategy. We don't want dropped requests or big latency spikes when traffic jumps. How do you handle burst capacity?
15:30 Samira: Good question. We offer two main patterns: 1) Reserved pool sized to average+headroom and autoscaling with pre-warm for sustained increases; 2) Hybrid bursting where short spikes are routed to hosted capacity with policy-based fallbacks. Fallbacks are model-compatible variants — e.g., 13B -> 7B for non-critical endpoints — or route to hosted for a short period. You can define SLO-based routing: prefer cost-saving until latency crosses threshold then fallback.

18:50 Derek: If we route to hosted for burst, will data leave our VPC?
18:55 Alex: If you need strict isolation, you'd pick Private deployment. Dedicated with hybrid bursting routes to Redwood-hosted endpoints and that does cross network boundaries; we can document egress and encryption in transit. For strict regulatory constraints you'd want a Private VPC/on-prem deployment.

21:15 Michael: What about autoscaling times — if we see a spike to 700 rps, how quickly can you add capacity? We can't afford 10-minute cold ramp.
21:28 Samira: Autoscaling has warm and cold components. Warm scaling from pre-warmed idle capacity can be sub-60s for some workloads; cold provisioning GPUs can be several minutes. Many customers configure reserved headroom plus warm standby nodes for predictable low-latency spikes. We'll quantify expected scale times in the sizing worksheet.

24:00 Linda: Encryption at rest requirements — we want envelope encryption via our KMS and HSM for keys. Is that supported?
24:07 Samira: Yes, BYOK via AWS KMS and support for HSM integrations available on Private deployments; for Dedicated we can support customer KMS in many setups — we'll check exact HSM compatibility.

26:20 Michael: Pricing — we need monthly committed cost estimates for budgeting. How do pricing and overage for bursts look?
26:30 Alex: Dedicated is committed monthly/annual pricing for reserved capacity; bursting to hosted is metered overage at per-token or per-inference rates. We'll send a worksheet that shows committed cost plus estimated overage scenarios based on your traffic.

28:05 Sonia (Procurement): Timeline question — if we move forward, what's typical lead time to provision Dedicated?
28:10 Alex: Typical lead time depends on network and security review, 2-6 weeks for standard VPC peering + reserved capacity. Private/on-prem is longer. For pilot with smaller reserved pool we can usually get started in 1-2 weeks.

31:00 Derek: Operationally, what telemetry do you expose? We want token-level latency, model-level throughput, per-route tracing, and cost breakdowns.
31:10 Jordan: Redwood Console includes token-level cost/latency breakdowns, per-model dashboards, tracing, and error analysis. We'll demo in a follow-up technical deep dive.

33:45 Michael: Our success criteria for this project: meet p95 < 150ms for fraud assistant in production, keep monthly inference cost within budget X (we shared ballpark), and achieve SOC2 compliance with retention and KMS controls. If those are met we plan for a Q3 rollout.
33:58 Alex: Understood. We'll map sizing and pricing to those criteria.

36:20 Linda: A quick question on model pinning/rollouts — how are canary rollouts handled? We need the ability to A/B test model versions without impacting production.
36:29 Samira: We support canary rollouts and A/B routes; you can pin traffic % to a new model and set automatic fallback if error or latency regressions are detected. We also support integration with your CI to trigger rollouts.

39:00 Michael: Any red flags? Where should we be cautious?
39:06 Alex: Biggest trade-offs are cost vs latency — to guarantee low p95 you pay for reserved headroom. Also, if you need strict geographic isolation or on-prem HSMs, that adds lead time. We'll surface those trade-offs in the worksheet.

41:20 Samira: For the benchmark, would you be able to provide a one-hour sample workload (replay) or synthetic load to mimic peak bursts? That will help us measure p95, throughput, and GPU counts.
41:30 Michael: Yes, we can provide a replay and also some telemetry. We'll coordinate offline — Derek will lead.

42:05 Alex: Great, to recap next steps: I'll send pricing and sizing worksheet; Samira will send benchmark plan and request sample workload; Linda will send compliance/KMS details; Michael/Derek will share traffic profiles. We'll target the technical deep dive / benchmarking session the week of 2026-04-27.
42:25 Linda: Sounds good. Sonia will follow up on procurement timeline.

43:10 Jordan: We'll also attach SOC2 docs and a short architecture note for VPC peering and egress.

44:00 Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and schedule.
44:06 Michael: Thanks Alex. Appreciate it.

End of transcript.
